slots.overviewDescription: Rivet in context: who runs it, the databases it reads, the bucket it writes and the warehouses it loads.
slots.mapDescription: The modules of the rivet binary, the state store and the outside systems, with the paths a batch export, a change capture, a warehouse load and a verification take.
slots.completionIntro: You followed one batch export from the command line to a manifest in the bucket, watched a change stream acknowledge only what was durable, and loaded the result into a warehouse behind a count gate.
slots.completionLessons:
• Why parts land first, the manifest second and the cursor last
  • Why a change is acknowledged at the source only after its part and manifest are durable
  • How rivet load trusts manifests and a row count, not whatever sits in the bucket
  • Where the state database fits: leases, ledgers and resume points

panels.introHtml:
Start here

Rivet, a production-database extractor

A map of rivet-lab/rivet in C4 terms. Rivet is one Rust command line tool: it reads PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB or Oracle, writes Parquet or CSV to local disk, S3, GCS or Azure, and can load the result into BigQuery, Snowflake or ClickHouse.

Rivet is made by the Rivet contributors and released under the MIT licence. This map describes it in its own words and is not affiliated with its authors.

Try it

  • Open a card to see that part of the tool.
  • Play Batch export: the order of the writes is the design.
  • Click a component for what it does and which files hold it.
panels.overviewHtml:
The full map

One binary, three outside worlds

There is no server: every box inside the system boundary is a module of the rivet binary, run once per command by cron, Airflow or a person. What survives between runs is the state database and the files in the bucket.

How to read it

People on the left, then the command layer, the batch and change-capture pipelines, the commit seam and state, and the warehouse loader. Source databases, the bucket, the warehouses and Slack are outside the boundary.

A second small binary, rivet-mcp, gives an AI agent read-only diagnostics on the source.

people.title: Operators and agents
people.line1: People or a scheduler run it.
people.text: Rivet runs as a command you schedule, not a hosted service. A data engineer writes rivet.yaml and a scheduler runs the commands; an AI agent can query source health through rivet-mcp.

sources.title: Source databases
sources.text: The operational databases rivet extracts from: by SQL reads for batch exports, and by their change logs for change data capture.

command.title: Commands and plans
command.text: The command line, the YAML config, the plan that turns an export into a concrete strategy, the init and doctor commands, and the separate MCP binary.

batch.title: Batch extract
batch.text: The export runner and its strategies, the per-engine source drivers and the sink that streams Arrow batches into temporary Parquet or CSV files.

cdc.title: Change capture
cdc.text: One change stream per engine and the capture sink that writes typed change parts and acknowledges the source only after they are durable.

durable.title: Commit and proof
durable.text: The commit seam that uploads parts and writes the manifest, the destination backends, the state database, and the validate, reconcile and repair commands that check what landed.

load.title: Warehouse load
load.text: The load driver that turns successful runs into warehouse tables, one adapter per warehouse, and the compact command that folds a change buffer into its base table.

outside.title: Storage and warehouses
outside.text: The object store or local folder that holds the exported parts, the warehouses rivet loads, and the Slack webhook it notifies.

nodes.what: Writes rivet.yaml (often scaffolded by rivet init) and runs rivet run, rivet load and rivet compact by hand or on a schedule.
nodes.why: Rivet is a command, not a platform: each invocation does one job and exits, so cron, Airflow, a Kubernetes CronJob or docker run can drive it.
nodes.tools: rivet binary · Homebrew, cargo or the Docker image · rivet.yaml

nodes.what: An assistant such as Claude Desktop or Claude Code that starts rivet-mcp and calls its tools to look at the source before or during an extract.
nodes.why: Lets an agent check sessions, locks and table stats on the source without being given write access to it.

nodes.tool: PostgreSQL · MySQL · SQL Server · MongoDB · Oracle
nodes.what: The production databases rivet reads. Batch exports send SQL (a server-side cursor on PostgreSQL, keyset or chunked range queries elsewhere); change capture reads a logical replication slot, the MySQL binlog, SQL Server change tables, a MongoDB change stream or Oracle LogMiner.
nodes.why: They are production, so rivet keeps reads short and bounded, detects connection poolers (pgBouncer, ProxySQL, the Azure SQL gateway) and measures the load it adds to the server.
nodes.tools: postgres · mysql · tiberius · mongodb crates · Oracle behind the oracle feature

nodes.what: Parses the arguments with clap, checks cross-flag rules, then dispatch matches the subcommand to its entry point: run, cdc, load, compact, init, check, doctor, plan, apply, validate, reconcile, repair and the state tools.
nodes.why: One place maps every error to an exit class and an error code, redacts credentials from the message and prints it as text or JSON, so schedulers can react to the exit status.

nodes.what: Reads rivet.yaml: the source, the list of exports with their mode, query, format and destination, tuning, notifications and the load: block. Resolves URLs from environment variables or files and applies --param values.
nodes.why: Everything rivet does is declared here, so validation and lints run before any connection is opened.

nodes.what: Turns one export into a ResolvedRunPlan: the extraction strategy (snapshot, incremental, time window, chunked, keyset), the tuning profile, column overrides and the destination. rivet plan seals the same plan into a file that rivet apply replays.
nodes.why: Separating the decision from the execution lets a plan be reviewed, hashed and replayed with the same chunk boundaries.

nodes.what: rivet init reads the source catalog and writes a reviewed YAML with one export per table and a suggested mode. rivet check runs EXPLAIN and a type report; rivet doctor probes the source and destination connections.
nodes.why: Most failures are a wrong URL, a missing grant or a type that will not survive; finding them before the first run saves a failed production extract.

nodes.what: A second binary that speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdin and stdout and exposes read-only tools: PostgreSQL sessions, checkpoint pressure, table stats, locks and top queries, and MySQL process list, key metrics and table stats.
nodes.why: Kept as its own binary rather than a subcommand, so an agent integration never pulls in the export path.

nodes.what: pipeline::run selects the exports, runs them one after another, on a thread pool or as child processes, and prints the run aggregate. For each export run_export_job either hands a mode: cdc export to the capture or runs the batch plan with its gates.
nodes.why: This is where the ordering lives: lease, run ledger, data, manifest, cursor, metrics. A crash between any two steps leaves something resume can finish rather than a gap.

nodes.what: run_with_reconnect retries a failed attempt with backoff and a fresh connection. run_export then picks the loop: one query (snapshot, incremental, time window), chunked ranges with optional per-chunk checkpoints, or keyset pages.
nodes.why: Short, bounded reads keep a large table from holding one long transaction on production; chunk and page checkpoints let --resume finish a crashed run.

nodes.what: One Source per engine. PostgreSQL declares a cursor and fetches N rows at a time; MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB and Oracle have their own loops. Each maps native types to a RivetType, converts rows to Arrow and pushes each batch to the sink. A shared batch controller sizes batches to a memory budget and throttles.
nodes.why: Adding an engine means implementing one trait; the rest of the pipeline only ever sees Arrow batches.

nodes.what: Receives the schema and each Arrow batch, adds meta columns, and streams them into a temporary Parquet or CSV file. It rotates to a new part at max_file_size and computes per-column checksums as it goes. By default a worker thread encodes while the source thread keeps fetching.
nodes.why: No batch is held beyond the current fetch, so memory stays at about batch size times row width, whatever the table size.

nodes.what: create_change_stream opens the engine's stream: on PostgreSQL a logical slot with the test_decoding plugin, polled with SQL (pg_logical_slot_peek_changes); the MySQL binlog; SQL Server change tables; a MongoDB change stream; Oracle LogMiner. Each yields canonical ChangeEvents with an operation, table, row image and resume position.
nodes.why: ack is separate from reading: an engine that consumes on read, like a PostgreSQL slot, only moves forward once rivet says the change is stored.
nodes.tools: src/source/cdc/mod.rs · src/source/postgres/cdc.rs · src/source/mysql/cdc.rs · large transactions spill to disk · a pgoutput decoder (pgoutput.rs) exists but is not yet used outside tests

nodes.what: run_capture resolves each captured table's columns, then run_to_files pulls changes, routes them to per-table buffers and rolls them into typed parts with __op, __pos and __seq columns. Each roll uploads and records the parts, rewrites the manifest, saves the checkpoint file and acks. The standalone rivet cdc command drives the same run_capture from a URL, without a state store.
nodes.why: Checkpoints sit on transaction boundaries and the ack comes last, so a crash anywhere re-reads changes instead of losing them: at-least-once. The resume position lives in a local checkpoint file (cdc.checkpoint, scaffolded as ./cdc/<table>.ckpt), not in the state database; on PostgreSQL the slot itself also holds it.

nodes.what: Uploads each sealed part, computes its xxh3 fingerprint and MD5, compares the MD5 with what the store reported, and records the part. At the end of the run it writes manifest.json listing every part with rows and checksums, and _SUCCESS when the run succeeded.
nodes.why: Every runner goes through the same seam, so the rule "file first, then the record of it" cannot drift between strategies. The manifest is what loaders trust.

nodes.what: create_destination builds local, stdout, S3, GCS or Azure. The cloud ones go through OpenDAL with a retry layer. Besides write, each can list, read and head objects so validate and resume can inspect a prefix.
nodes.why: A destination says how it commits (atomic, finalize on close, streaming); state is only updated once that commit is confirmed.

nodes.what: .rivet_state.db beside the config, or a PostgreSQL database when RIVET_STATE_URL is set. Holds incremental cursors, chunk checkpoints, the run-status ledger, the per-part file log, metrics, journals and the load ledger. The CDC resume position is not here: it is a separate checkpoint file beside the config.
nodes.why: Without it every run is a full reload and a crash means starting over. It is also what lets rivet load know which runs are already in the warehouse.

nodes.what: rivet validate re-reads a prefix's manifest and parts and checks counts and checksums without touching the source. rivet reconcile recounts each stored chunk with COUNT(*) on the source. rivet repair --execute re-exports only the chunks that differ.
nodes.why: A green exit code says the run finished, not that the data is right; these commands give a reason to believe the files.

nodes.what: rivet load plans one load per export, then for each table on a worker pool: takes a table lease, reads every manifest under the prefix, picks the successful runs not yet loaded, has the adapter land them and checks the row count before cleaning anything up.
nodes.why: The warehouse-neutral driver owns the order and the gates, so each warehouse adapter only has to know its own SQL. A load: block on a destination its warehouse cannot read (anything but GCS for BigQuery and Snowflake) is refused at plan time.

nodes.what: One TargetLoader per warehouse: materialize a table from Parquet, append_changelog for change data, create_view for the current-state view, compact and row_count. BigQuery uses its REST jobs API, Snowflake its SQL API with a key-pair JWT, ClickHouse its HTTP interface.
nodes.why: Every warehouse difference (external stages, partition limits, MERGE or not) stays behind this trait.

nodes.what: rivet compact merges each table's change buffer <table>__changes into its base table and drops the buffer. BigQuery uses MERGE statements, split into windows for partitioned tables; Snowflake runs a DELETE and an INSERT in one transaction.
nodes.why: Keeps the warehouse following the source with no full reloads. ClickHouse needs no compact step: its change log is a ReplacingMergeTree behind a view.
nodes.tools: src/load/compact.rs · runs on the same worker pool and ledger as load

nodes.tool: S3 · GCS · Azure Blob · local disk
nodes.what: Holds each export's prefix: the Parquet or CSV parts, named per run so a re-run never overwrites the last, plus manifest.json and _SUCCESS.
nodes.why: It is both the output and the hand-off to the warehouse: rivet load reads only what a successful manifest declares, and BigQuery and Snowflake read the parts straight from it, so a load into them needs a GCS destination.
nodes.tools: OpenDAL clients · credentials from the environment or files

nodes.what: Where the loaded tables live: a base table per export, a __changes change log or buffer for change data, and a current-state view over it. BigQuery (LOAD DATA) and Snowflake (storage integration) read the Parquet parts from GCS themselves; for ClickHouse rivet reads each part and sends it over HTTP, from GCS, S3 or Azure.
nodes.why: The reason most users run rivet at all; the dataset or database must already exist, rivet does not create it.
nodes.tools: BigQuery jobs API · Snowflake SQL API v2 · ClickHouse HTTP

nodes.what: Receives a short message with the export name, status, rows and duration when a run matches the configured events, such as a failure.
nodes.why: A scheduled tool that fails quietly is worse than none; the webhook URL can come from an environment variable.

batch.title: Batch export
batch.desc: One rivet run of a snapshot or incremental export: rows become Arrow batches, then Parquet parts, then a manifest, and only then is the cursor moved.

hops.t: A scheduler runs rivet run -c rivet.yaml. run_binary installs a logger that redacts passwords and hands the parsed command to dispatch.
dispatch_run parses the --param values and the config is loaded with them; RunSet picks the exports to run.
pipeline::run decides how to run the exports: one after another, on threads, or as child processes. It opens the state database first so its migrations run once.
For each export, build_plan_on resolves the plan: the strategy, the tuning profile and the destination.
execute_resolved_plan claims a run lease so two runs of one export cannot overlap, and writes a running row to the run-status ledger.
run_with_reconnect opens a source connection and calls run_export; a transient failure retries with backoff, a closed port fails at once with a pointer to rivet doctor.
A single-query strategy builds an ExportRequest with the query and, for incremental, the stored cursor, and calls Source::export.
PostgreSQL: inside a transaction, a server-side cursor and FETCH of N rows at a time. The batch size adapts to a memory budget and the loop can sleep between fetches.
Each batch is converted to Arrow and pushed to the sink. By default a worker thread encodes Parquet while the source thread fetches the next batch.
When the source is drained the writer is finished. Parts rotated at max_file_size and the last temp file are handed to write_sink_parts.
write_part_file uploads each part, then computes its fingerprint and MD5. If the store reported its own checksum and it differs, the run stops: the part corrupted in transit.
OpenDAL writes the object to S3, GCS or Azure, or the file lands in a local folder. Part names carry the run, so a re-run never overwrites the previous one.
record_part adds the part to the run's manifest list and to the file log in the state database.
finalize_manifest writes manifest.json with every part, row count and checksum, then _SUCCESS if the run succeeded.

store_journal saves the run journal and the run-status row is closed. Only then is the incremental cursor advanced, and only if the run succeeded with a manifest; a crash before it re-exports the window instead of skipping it. The metrics row comes last.
If notifications are configured and the outcome matches, a short message goes to the Slack webhook.

cdc.title: Change capture run
cdc.desc: A mode: cdc export drains the database's change log to its current end, writing typed change parts and acknowledging the source only after each part is durable.

hops.t: The same rivet run, on a config whose export has mode: cdc. The first run takes a baseline snapshot through the batch path; later runs only read changes.
run_export_job sees the CDC mode and takes the capture branch instead of the batch plan.

A CDC run lease in the state store keeps two runs of the export apart. The checkpoint is claimed by an owner file (<checkpoint>.owner) beside the checkpoint file, which stops two configs, each with its own state database, from reading the same stream.
run_cdc_export fills a CdcCapture with one output per captured table and calls run_capture.
create_change_stream opens the engine's stream from its last position. Tables whose log would carry only partial row images are refused before anything is read.

The stream reads the log: on PostgreSQL a test_decoding slot polled with pg_logical_slot_peek_changes, the binlog on MySQL, change tables on SQL Server, a change stream on MongoDB, LogMiner on Oracle.
next_change yields canonical changes. The sink routes each to its table's buffer and remembers the last transaction boundary it saw.
When the buffers are big enough, roll_all encodes each table's part and uploads it, one worker per table.
The parts land in the table's prefix.
Each part is recorded in the state database right after its upload, even if a sibling table's upload failed, so a failed run still says what it captured.
At a transaction boundary the run's manifest is rewritten to cover every part so far, still without _SUCCESS; the terminal write at a clean end adds it.
Only now: save the checkpoint file at the last commit boundary, then ack. On PostgreSQL this is what lets the slot move past the changes; a crash before it re-reads them.

load.title: Load the warehouse
load.desc: rivet load reads the manifests under each export's prefix, lands the runs not yet loaded and refuses to clean up unless the warehouse holds exactly the rows the manifests declare.

hops.t: After rivet run, the scheduler runs rivet load -c cdc.yaml.
run_loads plans one load per export from the config and picks one run id for the whole invocation, used as a cost label in the warehouse.
Each worker takes a lease on its target table, so two loads cannot append the same runs twice, and reads the load ledger.
prepare_load reads every manifest.json under the prefix, refuses foreign or failed runs and runs whose parts are no longer listed under the prefix, and keeps the successful runs not yet loaded.
The adapter for the target is built. A full export is materialized as a table; a CDC or incremental export is appended to <table>__changes.
BigQuery runs a query job through its REST API, Snowflake a SQL script through the SQL API, ClickHouse an INSERT … FORMAT Parquet per part.
BigQuery and Snowflake pull the Parquet parts straight from the GCS prefix; the data does not pass through rivet. (ClickHouse is the exception: rivet reads each part and sends it.)
The landed row count is read back from the target. check_loaded_rows compares it with the rows the manifests declared; on a mismatch the load fails and nothing is cleaned up.
Only after the gate passes, and only if cleanup_source is on and no run is still writing there, the loaded parts are removed from the prefix.
The load is recorded in load_run and each source run in loaded_source_run, so the next load skips them.
On a base-and-buffer layout the scheduler then runs rivet compact.
run_compacts calls the adapter's compact for each table.
BigQuery merges the buffer into the base with MERGE statements, split into windows for partitioned tables; Snowflake runs a DELETE and an INSERT in one transaction. Then the buffer is dropped.

verify.title: Prove what landed
verify.desc: Between runs, validate re-reads the files, reconcile recounts the source chunk by chunk, and repair re-exports only the chunks that differ.

hops.t: An operator or a CI job runs rivet validate on an export.
The validate command expands the export's destination and runs the same manifest checks as rivet run --validate, with no source query and no state writes.
It reads manifest.json and the parts through the destination backend and checks that every part is there with its rows and checksums.
The reads go to the same prefix the run wrote: a missing or changed part shows up here.
rivet reconcile works on chunked exports with checkpoints: it lists the stored chunk tasks of the last run with their row counts.
For each chunk it runs SELECT COUNT(*) over the chunk's query on the source and reports matches and mismatches.
rivet repair --execute re-runs just the mismatched ranges through the chunked runner. The new files sit beside the originals; nothing is deleted or overwritten.

buildSteps.title: A query to a local file
buildSteps.text: Parse the command and the YAML, connect to one database, stream rows as Arrow batches into a Parquet file.
buildSteps.decision: Everything downstream sees Arrow batches; each engine only has to produce them.

buildSteps.title: Parts and a manifest in a bucket
buildSteps.text: Upload each part through one commit seam and finish the run with manifest.json and _SUCCESS.
buildSteps.decision: File first, then the record of it: a crash leaves an unlisted part, never a listed part that is missing.

buildSteps.title: Plans, strategies and state
buildSteps.text: Resolve each export to a strategy, run it with retries, and keep cursors, checkpoints and the run ledger in SQLite.
buildSteps.decision: The cursor moves only after the manifest is written, so an incremental run never skips rows it did not land.

buildSteps.title: Checks before and after
buildSteps.text: Scaffold and probe before the first run; validate, reconcile and repair after it; tell Slack when something fails.
buildSteps.decision: Verification commands read the destination and the source again instead of trusting the run's own report.

buildSteps.title: Change data capture
buildSteps.text: Read each engine's change log as canonical events and write them as typed change parts.
buildSteps.decision: Acknowledge the source last, after part, manifest and checkpoint: at-least-once instead of maybe-lost.

buildSteps.title: Into the warehouse
buildSteps.text: Load the runs a manifest declares, check the landed row count, then clean up; compact change buffers into base tables.
buildSteps.decision: A warehouse-neutral driver owns the gates; each adapter only knows its own SQL and API.
buildSteps.runnable: rivet load -c cdc.yaml && rivet compact -c cdc.yaml

buildSteps.title: Diagnostics for agents
buildSteps.text: A separate stdio binary exposes read-only source diagnostics as MCP tools.
buildSteps.decision: A separate binary, so an agent integration never links in the write path.

tour.title: One binary between production and the warehouse
body: Rivet copies tables from an operational database into files, and optionally into a warehouse. It runs as a command and exits; there is no server.
People and an AI agent on one side, the source databases, the bucket and the warehouses on the other, and in between five parts of one Rust binary.
tour.why: The source is production and the result has to be trusted, so most of the design is about the order of writes and the evidence each run leaves behind.

tour.title: From a command to rows
body: Follow one export from the command line through the plan and the retry loop to a cursor on the source.
tour.why: Leases and the run ledger are taken before any row is read, so a second scheduler tick cannot run the same export twice.

tour.title: Parts first, cursor last
body: Batches become Parquet parts, parts become objects, objects are listed in a manifest, and only then does the cursor move.
tour.why: A crash at any point leaves either data with no record, which resume picks up, or nothing; never a record that skips data.

tour.title: Changes, acknowledged when durable
body: A CDC run drains the log to its current end, rolling buffered changes into typed parts.
tour.why: On PostgreSQL the ack moves the slot for good, so it has to come after the part, the manifest and the checkpoint.

tour.title: Into the warehouse, behind a count gate
body: rivet load reads manifests, not the bucket listing, and compares the landed rows with what the manifests declare.
tour.why: A typo'd prefix or a half-written run would otherwise load silently; here it is refused before anything is cleaned up.

tour.title: Proof after the fact
body: Validate, reconcile and repair check the files and the source again, independently of the run that wrote them.
tour.why: These commands are why a green run can be believed: each one re-reads instead of trusting the run's own numbers.

tour.title: The whole tool, on one map

recap.people: A person or a scheduler runs the commands; an agent can ask about the source.
recap.command: Parse the command and config, plan each export, scaffold and probe.
recap.batch: Strategies drive source drivers; Arrow batches stream into Parquet or CSV parts.
recap.cdc: Change streams per engine; parts first, ack last.
recap.sources: Production databases, read in short bounded queries or through their logs.
recap.durable: One commit seam, a manifest per run, a state database, and checks after the fact.
recap.load: Manifests to warehouse tables behind a count gate, then compact.
recap.outside: The bucket that holds the parts, the warehouses, and Slack.

body: One Rust binary run per command, with the state database and the bucket as its only memory.
The design choice that shapes everything: each step writes its evidence before the next step is allowed to rely on it.

runner.title: Inside the runner: one batch export
runner.sub: What execute_resolved_plan in src/pipeline/job.rs does for one export, in order.
runner.cap: The data phase is one step in the middle. Everything after it decides what the run may claim: the manifest is written before the cursor moves, and the result is failed if any gate (validate, reconcile, cursor) failed, even when the data landed.

steps.d: A partitioned export must already be expanded; a MongoDB collection is bound to its incarnation.
Take the run lease, claim the progress row, recover an interrupted checkpoint run and refuse a stored cursor past the last manifest.

steps.t: Open the run in the ledger
steps.d: A running row in run_status, then column and harm snapshots on a metadata connection.
Temporal settle columns, the type policy (--strict) and a prefix written by another pipeline shape.
Parallel chunked with or without checkpoints, or run_with_reconnect for everything else.
On success, schema drift and quality checks; on failure, name a revoked column or a missing table.
Only when asked: count the source and compare with the rows exported.
manifest.json and _SUCCESS; a manifest that cannot be written turns the run into a failure.

steps.t: Store the journal and close the ledger row

steps.d: Only if the run succeeded with a manifest; otherwise the next run re-exports the window.
Failure, a manifest gap, or any of the validate, reconcile and cursor gates.

cdcsink.title: Inside the capture sink: one roll
cdcsink.sub: What roll_all in src/pipeline/cdc/sink.rs does each time the buffers are flushed.
cdcsink.cap: The order is the guarantee: parts, then manifest, then checkpoint, then ack. Every table is flushed before the stream position is acknowledged, because the position belongs to the whole stream, not to one table.

steps.t: Pick the tables with buffered changes

steps.d: The first roll for a table writes a manifest without _SUCCESS, so the prefix shows a run in progress.

steps.t: Encode and upload each table's part
steps.d: In parallel, one worker per table.
Even when a sibling's upload failed: it is durable either way.

exit.t: Stop without checkpoint or ack; the changes are read again

steps.d: A run-unique Success manifest that covers every part so far, still without _SUCCESS.
On PostgreSQL this lets the slot advance; it cannot be undone.

loaddriver.title: Inside the load driver: one table
loaddriver.sub: What execute_load in src/load/orchestrate.rs does for one table, with the full-load leg from run_load.
loaddriver.cap: Every refusal happens before the first warehouse write and is journaled as refused. Cleanup of the staged files is the last thing that can happen, and only after the count gate.

steps.d: Two loads of one table would both read the ledger before either wrote it.
Read and reconcile every manifest under the prefix, select the runs not yet loaded and sum their rows.

exit.t: Up to date, recorded as a skip

steps.d: Not a view where a base table belongs, owned by rivet, within the partition budget.

steps.t: Mark the load as writing and run the leg

steps.d: Landed rows must equal the manifests' rows.

exit.t: Load fails, source not cleaned up

steps.t: Record the load in the ledger

state.title: Inside the state store: the main tables
state.sub: Some of the tables from src/state/migrations.rs. The same ladder exists for SQLite and for PostgreSQL.
state.cap: Names are versioned by migrations: file_log was created as file_manifest and renamed in v8, when the word manifest was given to the JSON file in the bucket. Most tables are keyed by export name and run id, not by a foreign key.

tables.name: export_state
tables.note: One row per export: where an incremental export resumes.

tables.name: run_status
tables.note: The run ledger: running at start, terminal at finalize.

fields.note: which bucket prefix the run writes
the manifest's status is copied from here

tables.name: chunk_task
tables.note: Per-chunk checkpoint of a chunked run; reconcile reads its counts.

tables.name: chunk_run
tables.note: One chunked run; a partial unique index allows one in progress per export.

fields.note: a resume must match the plan

tables.name: export_metrics
tables.note: One row per run, failed runs included, for rivet metrics.

tables.name: load_run
tables.note: Audit log of rivet load: one row per invocation and table.

fields.note: the extraction runs this load consumed

tables.name: loaded_source_run
tables.note: The skip set: which extraction runs are already in which target.

entries.t: Thin entry point: calls cli::run_binary.
The clap grammar, cross-flag checks and the dispatch from subcommand to module.
entries.why: The grammar (args.rs) is kept apart from what each command does (dispatch.rs), so the CLI reference can be generated from it.

entries.t: rivet.yaml: source, exports, destinations, load block, lints and URL resolution.
Resolved run plans, sealed plan artifacts, advisory export prioritization and repair plans.
Orchestration: the run, the per-export job, strategies, sink, commit seam and the verification commands.
pipeline::run: selects exports and runs them sequentially, on threads or as child processes.
One export: CDC branch or the batch plan with its gates, manifest and cursor order.
entries.why: Read execute_resolved_plan first; it is the ordering contract of a batch run in one function.

entries.t: Retry and reconnect loop, the single-query export.
Chunked exports: range math, sequential and parallel runners, checkpoint resume.
ExportSink: temp files, part rotation, checksums, the pipelined encoder thread.
The commit seam: upload a part, check its MD5, record it. finalize.rs writes the manifest and marker at the end.
entries.why: Every runner calls the same two seams, so the write-then-record order cannot differ between strategies.

entries.t: The capture assembler and the change-part sink with its roll sequence.
